Multimodal freight transportation refers to the movement of goods using multiple modes of transportation (e.g., truck, rail, sea) under a single contract, typically without seamless integration between different modes and often requiring manual intervention for transitions . Intermodal freight transportation, in contrast, is characterized by more sophisticated coordination among different transport modes, where goods are moved in standardized containers across multiple modes within a single journey, optimizing the efficiency of transitions between modes . Synchromodal freight transportation represents the most advanced paradigm, integrating real-time data and dynamic decision-making capabilities that allow for the selection of the most suitable transport mode at each leg of the journey based on current conditions and customer requirements, thereby offering superior flexibility and efficiency compared to previous methods .

Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. Freight Transportation Paradigms

To establish clarity within our analytical framework, we first define and distinguish several interconnected logistics paradigms in the freight transportation sector. Within the domain of logistics and supply chain management, multimodal, intermodal, and synchromodal freight transportation represent distinct yet interconnected concepts that have evolved to address increasing complexity in global logistics networks.

Multimodal freight transportation refers to the movement of goods using multiple modes of transportation (e.g., truck, rail, sea) under a single contract, typically without seamless integration between different modes and often requiring manual intervention for transitions . Intermodal freight transportation, in contrast, is characterized by more sophisticated coordination among different transport modes, where goods are moved in standardized containers across multiple modes within a single journey, optimizing the efficiency of transitions between modes . Synchromodal freight transportation represents the most advanced paradigm, integrating real-time data and dynamic decision-making capabilities that allow for the selection of the most suitable transport mode at each leg of the journey based on current conditions and customer requirements, thereby offering superior flexibility and efficiency compared to previous methods .

Additional freight transportation paradigms include unimodal transportation (involving only one mode of transport), combined transport (specifically focusing on minimizing road usage by shifting to rail or inland waterways for long-distance segments), and co-modal transportation (promoting the efficient combination of transport modes without modal hierarchy) . Collectively, these paradigms represent the evolution of freight logistics toward increasingly integrated and adaptive systems designed to meet the demands of modern supply chains. Given that many of these paradigms represent progressive enhancements of their predecessors with extended capabilities, this paper focuses on an integrated freight transportation paradigm that incorporates recent generative AI techniques and their exceptional knowledge extraction and reasoning capabilities. This approach enables an automated methodology that leverages knowledge from previous paradigms to formulate adaptive solutions tailored to the nature and requirements of real-world decision problems in large-scale logistics systems.

 It is important to note that the extensive literature on multimodal, intermodal, and synchromodal freight optimization summarized above predominantly addresses the mathematical and algorithmic dimension of the problem (i.e., formulating and solving routing, scheduling, and mode-selection models), typically assuming that model formulation, data preparation, and solver or simulator execution are carried out manually by domain experts. The specific contribution of this paper is not a new freight optimization algorithm, but rather an agentic orchestration layer that autonomously performs these traditionally manual steps: interpreting a user's natural-language freight planning request, selecting an appropriate mathematical formulation and toolchain, and executing the resulting workflow end-to-end through MCP-coordinated agents. This distinguishes our work from the freight optimization literature summarized above, which largely treats the orchestration of tools and expertise as an implicit, human-performed step outside the scope of the proposed models.

This line of work is complementary to, rather than overlapping with, the contribution of the present paper: whereas network- and communication-layer digital twin research is primarily concerned with how a digital twin's state is transmitted and maintained efficiently, our agentic digital twin framework is primarily concerned with what an already-available digital twin autonomously does, i.e., how generative AI agents reason about, plan, and invoke domain-specific solvers and simulators once the twin's state and supporting data are accessible. Integrating bandwidth- and latency-aware communication strategies from this literature into the agent-communication layer of our framework, particularly for large-scale, multi-node deployments, is a promising direction for future work.

Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. In contrast, foundation models generalize effectively across domains, process unstructured data, and respond to novel tasks with minimal adjustment requirements . They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. Conventional methods often require manual configuration, structured data, and deep domain expertise, thereby limiting their flexibility and broader applicability. In contrast, foundation models generalize effectively across domains, process unstructured data, and respond to novel tasks with minimal adjustment requirements . They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . This fundamental shift enables accelerated discovery cycles and supports integrated, interdisciplinary research, thereby laying the groundwork for automating complex scientific workflows and accelerating knowledge generation processes.

Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . By enabling intelligent, autonomous agents to reason, plan, and coordinate across diverse data sources and scientific tools, this paradigm promises to transform digital twins into more adaptive, scalable, and automated systems for complex urban management.

Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. Conventional methods often require manual configuration, structured data, and deep domain expertise, thereby limiting their flexibility and broader applicability. In contrast, foundation models generalize effectively across domains, process unstructured data, and respond to novel tasks with minimal adjustment requirements . They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. Conventional methods often require manual configuration, structured data, and deep domain expertise, thereby limiting their flexibility and broader applicability. In contrast, foundation models generalize effectively across domains, process unstructured data, and respond to novel tasks with minimal adjustment requirements . They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . This fundamental shift enables accelerated discovery cycles and supports integrated, interdisciplinary research, thereby laying the groundwork for automating complex scientific workflows and accelerating knowledge generation processes.

This connection enables decision-makers to optimize route planning and dynamically adapt to disruptions, thereby improving overall system flexibility and efficiency. The integration of these digital and physical elements aims to facilitate a modal shift from road to more sustainable modes, such as rail and inland waterways, thereby contributing to environmental objectives by reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Digital Twins over Communication Networks

 A parallel and rapidly growing body of research addresses digital twins from a communication and networking perspective, focusing on how a digital twin's virtual state is efficiently created, updated, and delivered over resource-constrained wireless and edge networks, for example through semantic communication frameworks that compress and prioritize the information exchanged between physical assets and their digital counterparts, generative-AI-aided resource allocation strategies that preserve digital twin fidelity under uncertain channel conditions, and edge-computing deployment strategies that decide when and where to instantiate digital twin computations to meet real-time accuracy and latency requirements. This line of work is complementary to, rather than overlapping with, the contribution of the present paper: whereas network- and communication-layer digital twin research is primarily concerned with how a digital twin's state is transmitted and maintained efficiently, our agentic digital twin framework is primarily concerned with what an already-available digital twin autonomously does, i.e., how generative AI agents reason about, plan, and invoke domain-specific solvers and simulators once the twin's state and supporting data are accessible. Integrating bandwidth- and latency-aware communication strategies from this literature into the agent-communication layer of our framework, particularly for large-scale, multi-node deployments, is a promising direction for future work.

Despite their demonstrated value and significance, these digital twins are developed using conventional digital twinning approaches that exhibit several fundamental limitations. Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .

Compared to traditional simulation or statistical models, foundation models offer superior scalability, adaptability, and efficiency. Conventional methods often require manual configuration, structured data, and deep domain expertise, thereby limiting their flexibility and broader applicability. In contrast, foundation models generalize effectively across domains, process unstructured data, and respond to novel tasks with minimal adjustment requirements . They can analyze vast datasets, interpret complex visualizations, learn from recent literature, and propose new hypotheses with levels of insight and efficiency unmatched by traditional analytical tools . This fundamental shift enables accelerated discovery cycles and supports integrated, interdisciplinary research, thereby laying the groundwork for automating complex scientific workflows and accelerating knowledge generation processes.

Additional freight transportation paradigms include unimodal transportation (involving only one mode of transport), combined transport (specifically focusing on minimizing road usage by shifting to rail or inland waterways for long-distance segments), and co-modal transportation (promoting the efficient combination of transport modes without modal hierarchy) . Collectively, these paradigms represent the evolution of freight logistics toward increasingly integrated and adaptive systems designed to meet the demands of modern supply chains. Given that many of these paradigms represent progressive enhancements of their predecessors with extended capabilities, this paper focuses on an integrated freight transportation paradigm that incorporates recent generative AI techniques and their exceptional knowledge extraction and reasoning capabilities. This approach enables an automated methodology that leverages knowledge from previous paradigms to formulate adaptive solutions tailored to the nature and requirements of real-world decision problems in large-scale logistics systems.

Multi-agent System Paradigm

A multi-agent system (MAS) represents a computational framework composed of multiple autonomous agents, each possessing specialized capabilities, that interact and coordinate to achieve shared objectives or solve complex problems . These agents emulate collaborative behaviors observed in natural and human systems. When augmented with emerging AI technologies—particularly LLMs and RAG-they become powerful instruments for domain-specific reasoning, decision-making, and workflow orchestration. In the context of digital twins, MAS architectures have demonstrated increasing potential for enhancing system intelligence, scalability, and user-centricity. Recent research illustrates how LLM-based agents can serve as conversational interfaces, knowledge reasoners, and task coordinators, while task-specific agents handle specialized functions such as traffic simulation, optimization, or data retrieval . For instance, in urban mobility systems, a GenAI-powered multi-agent digital twin can autonomously interpret user-defined transportation scenarios, retrieve relevant real-time and historical data, and dynamically invoke simulation or optimization models—effectively transforming digital twins from passive data mirrors into active decision-support engines . This paradigm shift enables intelligent transportation systems to deliver personalized, science-based, and adaptive mobility services at scale.

Multi-agent Systems offer a powerful architectural paradigm for managing complexity, decentralization, and modularity in intelligent applications. One of the primary advantages of MAS lies in their ability to decompose complex tasks into coordinated subtasks, each handled by a specialized agent capable of autonomous decision-making and contextual reasoning . This capability enables scalability, fault-tolerance, and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments—key characteristics essential for next-generation digital twins. An emerging framework known as the MCP further enhances MAS by standardizing communication and coordination among heterogeneous agents and tools in scientific workflows. MCP introduces a structured, context-aware interface that allows agents to exchange model inputs, results, and metadata while preserving semantic interoperability . When integrated into MAS architectures, MCP enables digital twin platforms to seamlessly orchestrate complex workflows across simulation, optimization, and data services, transforming traditionally siloed tools into composable, interoperable services. This synergy transforms digital twins from passive mirrors of real-world systems into active cognitive platforms that can autonomously reason, plan, and optimize operations at scale.

Rise of Knowledge-Augmented LLMs as Generative Foundation Models

The emergence of generative AI models—including GPT-3, GPT-4, and DALL-E—has catalyzed the development of foundation models, fundamentally transforming scientific research across multiple disciplines . These large-scale, pre-trained models excel at understanding, generating, and synthesizing complex data types—including textual, visual, and multimodal content—and can be effectively adapted for diverse scientific tasks . Through training on extensive domain-specific corpora, including scientific literature, experimental results, and multimodal datasets, foundation models support critical tasks such as knowledge extraction, data analysis, hypothesis generation, simulation, and systems-level data integration .

Unlike traditional domain-specific models, foundation models represent a paradigm shift from bespoke machine learning solutions to general-purpose, adaptable architectures . They learn transferable representations that can be fine-tuned for specialized use cases across domains, including medicine, climate science, and urban systems . Current applications include BERT-based models in chemistry , LLMs for biomedical synthesis , and multimodal models for geoinformatics and remote sensing .
